Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE‑754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. The operation itself is mathematically associative: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). However, on modern hardware the actual sequence of operations can differ in several subtle ways that break this property. First, each addition produces an intermediate result that may be rounded to the nearest representable number; if two different orders of summation are performed, the rounding errors introduced at each step accumulate differently. Second, many processors employ fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions or other optimizations that compute a product and sum in a single operation with only one final rounding. When an addition is performed separately from its preceding multiplication, the intermediate result may be rounded earlier than it would have been if the FMA were used. Third, hardware often uses extended precision registers (such as 80‑bit or 128‑bit internal formats) to hold intermediate results before they are stored back into a 64‑bit double. The compiler and runtime can choose whether to keep values in these wider registers or to truncate them early; different compilation options or even different instruction scheduling decisions can lead to distinct rounding points. Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of these factors, floating‑point addition is not associative on real hardware: the result of (a + b) + c may differ by one unit in the last place from a + (b + c). In isolation this difference is tiny, but when thousands or millions of such operations are chained together—as in large matrix multiplications—the errors can accumulate and propagate. Matrix multiplication typically involves summing many products: each entry of the result matrix is computed as a dot product of two vectors, requiring a reduction over n terms. The order in which these partial sums are combined determines the pattern of rounding errors. If one implementation reduces left‑to‑right while another reduces right‑to‑left, or if they use different tree structures for parallel reductions, the intermediate sums will be rounded at different points and with different magnitudes. Even a single extra rounding can change the sign of a tiny error term that later influences subsequent operations.

When large matrices are multiplied on multi‑core systems, the reduction order is often decided by the parallel algorithm employed. A naive serial implementation might use a straightforward loop nest, whereas a highly optimized library could employ blocking, vectorization, and tree‑based reductions to exploit cache locality and SIMD units. Each of these strategies imposes its own summation pattern. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, two runs that differ only in the reduction order can produce slightly different final matrices. In many scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable; however, for reproducibility—especially when results are compared across different hardware or software stacks—even a single bit difference can cause downstream algorithms to diverge. This sensitivity becomes more pronounced as matrix sizes grow and the number of operations increases, making it essential to understand that floating‑point arithmetic does not guarantee identical outcomes under all reduction orders.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE 754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

The operation itself is mathematically associative: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). However, on modern hardware the actual sequence of operations can differ in several subtle ways that break this property. First, each addition produces an intermediate result that may be rounded to the nearest representable number; if two different orders of summation are performed, the rounding errors introduced at each step accumulate differently. Second, many processors employ fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions or other optimizations that compute a product and sum in a single operation with only one final rounding. When an addition is performed separately from its preceding multiplication, the intermediate result may be rounded earlier than it would have been if the FMA were used. Third, hardware often uses extended precision registers (such as 80‑bit or 128‑bit internal formats) to hold intermediate results before they are stored back into a 64‑bit double. The compiler and runtime can choose whether to keep values in these wider registers or to truncate them early; different compilation options or even different instruction scheduling decisions can lead to distinct rounding points. Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of these factors, floating‑point addition is not associative on real hardware: the result of (a + b) + c may differ by one unit in the last place from a + (b + c). Matrix multiplication typically involves summing many products: each entry of the result matrix is computed as a dot product of two vectors, requiring a reduction over n terms. The order in which these partial sums are combined determines the pattern of rounding errors. If one implementation reduces left‑to‑right while another reduces right‑to‑left, or if they use different tree structures for parallel reductions, the intermediate sums will be rounded at different points and with different magnitudes. Even a single extra rounding can change the sign of a tiny error term that later influences subsequent operations.

Because floating‑point addition is not associative, two runs that differ only in the reduction order can produce slightly different final matrices. In many scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable; however, for reproducibility—especially when results are compared across different hardware or software stacks—even a single bit difference can cause downstream algorithms to diverge. This sensitivity becomes more pronounced as matrix sizes grow and the number of operations increases, making it essential to understand that floating‑point arithmetic does not guarantee identical outcomes under all reduction orders.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE 754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

First, each addition produces an intermediate result that may be rounded to the nearest representable number; if two different orders of summation are performed, the rounding errors introduced at each step accumulate differently. Second, many processors employ fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions or other optimizations that compute a product and sum in a single operation with only one final rounding. When an addition is performed separately from its preceding multiplication, the intermediate result may be rounded earlier than it would have been if the FMA were used. Third, hardware often uses extended precision registers (such as 80‑bit or 128‑bit internal formats) to hold intermediate results before they are stored back into a 64‑bit double. The compiler and runtime can choose whether to keep values in these wider registers or to truncate them early; different compilation options or even different instruction scheduling decisions can lead to distinct rounding points. Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of these factors, floating‑point addition is not associative on real hardware: the result of (a + b) + c may differ by one unit in the last place from a + (b + c). In isolation this difference is tiny, but when thousands or millions of such operations are chained together—as in large matrix multiplications—the errors can accumulate and propagate. Matrix multiplication typically involves summing many products: each entry of the result matrix is computed as a dot product of two vectors, requiring a reduction over n terms. The order in which these partial sums are combined determines the pattern of rounding errors. If one implementation reduces left‑to‑right while another reduces right‑to‑left, or if they use different tree structures for parallel reductions, the intermediate sums will be rounded at different points and with different magnitudes. Even a single extra rounding can change the sign of a tiny error term that later influences subsequent operations.

Each of these strategies imposes its own summation pattern. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, two runs that differ only in the reduction order can produce slightly different final matrices. In many scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable; however, for reproducibility—especially when results are compared across different hardware or software stacks—even a single bit difference can cause downstream algorithms to diverge. This sensitivity becomes more pronounced as matrix sizes grow and the number of operations increases, making it essential to understand that floating‑point arithmetic does not guarantee identical outcomes under all reduction orders.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE 754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE‑754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. The operation itself is mathematically associative: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). However, on modern hardware the actual sequence of operations can differ in several subtle ways that break this property. First, each addition produces an intermediate result that may be rounded to the nearest representable number; if two different orders of summation are performed, the rounding errors introduced at each step accumulate differently. Second, many processors employ fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions or other optimizations that compute a product and sum in a single operation with only one final rounding. When an addition is performed separately from its preceding multiplication, the intermediate result may be rounded earlier than it would have been if the FMA were used. Third, hardware often uses extended precision registers (such as 80‑bit or 128‑bit internal formats) to hold intermediate results before they are stored back into a 64‑bit double. The compiler and runtime can choose whether to keep values in these wider registers or to truncate them early; different compilation options or even different instruction scheduling decisions can lead to distinct rounding points. Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of these factors, floating‑point addition is not associative on real hardware: the result of (a + b) + c may differ by one unit in the last place from a + (b + c). In isolation this difference is tiny, but when thousands or millions of such operations are chained together—as in large matrix multiplications—the errors can accumulate and propagate. Matrix multiplication typically involves summing many products: each entry of the result matrix is computed as a dot product of two vectors, requiring a reduction over n terms. The order in which these partial sums are combined determines the pattern of rounding errors. If one implementation reduces left‑to‑right while another reduces right‑to‑left, or if they use different tree structures for parallel reductions, the intermediate sums will be rounded at different points and with different magnitudes. Even a single extra rounding can change the sign of a tiny error term that later influences subsequent operations.

When large matrices are multiplied on multi‑core systems, the reduction order is often decided by the parallel algorithm employed. A naive serial implementation might use a straightforward loop nest, whereas a highly optimized library could employ blocking, vectorization, and tree‑based reductions to exploit cache locality and SIMD units. Each of these strategies imposes its own summation pattern. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, two runs that differ only in the reduction order can produce slightly different final matrices. In many scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable; however, for reproducibility—especially when results are compared across different hardware or software stacks—even a single bit difference can cause downstream algorithms to diverge. This sensitivity becomes more pronounced as matrix sizes grow and the number of operations increases, making it essential to understand that floating‑point arithmetic does not guarantee identical outcomes under all reduction orders.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE 754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE 754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. Because of this rounding step, the exact real number obtained from adding two operands is not preserved; instead, an approximation is stored in the finite precision format. When three or more numbers are added together, the order in which the pairwise sums are performed determines which intermediate results are rounded and how many times each operand participates in a rounding operation. In other words, the expression (a + b) + c may produce a different final value than a + (b + c), even though mathematically they are identical. This lack of associativity is inherent to any finite‑precision representation and cannot be eliminated by hardware design alone.

Modern processors implement floating‑point addition with microarchitectural optimizations that further exacerbate the non‑associative behavior. Many CPUs use fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions, which compute a × b + c in a single step with only one rounding at the end. When an algorithm is written to exploit FMAs, the compiler may transform a sequence of separate additions and multiplications into a fused form, thereby changing the reduction order implicitly. Even when FMAs are not used, hardware pipelines often perform partial sums in parallel or reorder operations for performance reasons. The result is that two executions of the same high‑level algorithm on identical data can diverge if they follow different instruction schedules or use different vector widths.

Large matrix multiplications typically involve summing many products across rows and columns. In a naive implementation, one might accumulate partial sums in a single scalar variable, but more efficient approaches distribute the accumulation across multiple registers or threads to reduce memory traffic and improve cache locality. Each of these strategies defines a distinct reduction tree: a binary tree of pairwise additions that determines which partial results are combined first. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, different trees produce slightly different final sums. When many such sums are aggregated—such as in the dot products that form each entry of the output matrix—the small discrepancies can accumulate and lead to noticeable differences between runs.

Reproducibility becomes a practical concern when scientific simulations or machine learning training pipelines rely on deterministic results. If two executions use different reduction orders, they may produce outputs that differ by more than the expected numerical noise, potentially affecting convergence diagnostics or model evaluation metrics. Even in a single run, parallel reductions across multiple cores can interleave operations unpredictably, especially if thread scheduling is non‑deterministic. The effect is amplified when the matrices are large because each element’s value depends on thousands of floating‑point additions; any change in rounding order propagates through the entire result.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a strict reduction order by using tree‑structured summations that are independent of execution context, or they employ higher precision accumulators such as double‑double or quadruple precision to reduce rounding errors. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize reductions or use deterministic algorithms at the cost of performance. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition remains a source of variability in large matrix multiplications executed with different reduction orders on modern hardware.

Floating‑point addition is defined by the IEEE‑754 standard to produce a result that is rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. The operation itself is mathematically associative: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). However, on modern hardware the actual sequence of operations can differ in several subtle ways that break this property. First, each addition produces an intermediate result that may be rounded to the nearest representable number; if two different orders of summation are performed, the rounding errors introduced at each step accumulate differently. Second, many processors employ fused multiply‑add (FMA) instructions or other optimizations that compute a product and sum in a single operation with only one final rounding. When an addition is performed separately from its preceding multiplication, the intermediate result may be rounded earlier than it would have been if the FMA were used. Third, hardware often uses extended precision registers (such as 80‑bit or 128‑bit internal formats) to hold intermediate results before they are stored back into a 64‑bit double. The compiler and runtime can choose whether to keep values in these wider registers or to truncate them early; different compilation options or even different instruction scheduling decisions can lead to distinct rounding points. Finally, the presence of parallel execution units means that independent additions may be performed out of order, with the processor reordering instructions for performance while preserving program semantics only at a higher level. This reordering can change which operands are summed first and thus alter the sequence of roundings.

Because of these factors, floating‑point addition is not associative on real hardware: the result of (a + b) + c may differ by one unit in the last place from a + (b + c). In isolation this difference is tiny, but when thousands or millions of such operations are chained together—as in large matrix multiplications—the errors can accumulate and propagate. Matrix multiplication typically involves summing many products: each entry of the result matrix is computed as a dot product of two vectors, requiring a reduction over n terms. The order in which these partial sums are combined determines the pattern of rounding errors. If one implementation reduces left‑to‑right while another reduces right‑to‑left, or if they use different tree structures for parallel reductions, the intermediate sums will be rounded at different points and with different magnitudes. Even a single extra rounding can change the sign of a tiny error term that later influences subsequent operations.

When large matrices are multiplied on multi‑core systems, the reduction order is often decided by the parallel algorithm employed. A naive serial implementation might use a straightforward loop nest, whereas a highly optimized library could employ blocking, vectorization, and tree‑based reductions to exploit cache locality and SIMD units. Each of these strategies imposes its own summation pattern. Because floating‑point addition is not associative, two runs that differ only in the reduction order can produce slightly different final matrices. In many scientific applications this discrepancy is acceptable; however, for reproducibility—especially when results are compared across different hardware or software stacks—even a single bit difference can cause downstream algorithms to diverge. This sensitivity becomes more pronounced as matrix sizes grow and the number of operations increases, making it essential to understand that floating‑point arithmetic does not guarantee identical outcomes under all reduction orders.
